This study introduces a time-dependent Poisson autoregressive model, termed TDPAR(p), designed to capture temporal variations in the persistence of count data. Unlike conventional Poisson autoregressive models that rely on fixed-order parameters, the TDPAR(p) model incorporates a time-varying parameter, denoted as $\gamma_t$, which represents the effective order of the process. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the TDPAR(p) process and derive its asymptotic properties. Furthermore, we propose a consistent estimator for the model's parameters and develop a testing procedure to determine the appropriate value of $p$. The efficacy of the TDPAR(p) model and its associated estimation and testing methods is demonstrated through both simulated data and real-world applications. Additionally, we introduce a new measure of persistence for count data and utilize it to evaluate the performance of the TDPAR(p) model. The results indicate that the TDPAR(p) model effectively captures the time-varying persistence observed in the data. Finally, we apply the TDPAR(p) model to analyze the persistence of daily COVID-19 case counts across 100 countries. The findings reveal that the persistence of these counts varies significantly by country and over time, with a general trend of decreasing persistence as the pandemic progresses. These insights offer valuable guidance for policymakers regarding the timing and intensity of interventions required to control the spread of the virus. The proposed model and associated methodologies are applicable to a wide range of count data scenarios. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/chenyuan1990/TDPAR.

This study introduces a novel technique for quantifying atmospheric aerosols by leveraging the photometric variability of stars. The method relies on the optical depth of aerosols, which causes a uniform dimming of stellar light. By analyzing the light curves of variable stars, we can derive the optical depth of the overlying atmosphere. We applied this approach to a dataset of 1,000 variable stars collected by the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System (ATLAS) between 2015 and 2019. The resulting optical depth values were compared against measurements from the AERONET network, yielding a correlation coefficient of 0.75. Furthermore, we utilized the derived optical depths to estimate aerosol concentrations, which were then validated against data from the Community Atmospheric Model version 4.8 (CAM4.8). The findings indicate that the concentration estimates align well with the model outputs. This new method offers a cost-effective means of monitoring atmospheric aerosols, potentially serving as a valuable tool for future space-based missions. Additionally, it provides a practical solution for calibrating the optical depth of aerosols in the light curves of exoplanet host stars, which is essential for accurately determining exoplanet sizes. This study introduces a new metric for assessing image captioning systems, termed the human benchmark score. This metric leverages a collection of high-quality captions created by human experts to serve as a reference standard. We introduce a dataset comprising 1,000 images, each annotated with a caption by a specialist in the field. We introduce a novel method to quantify the intricacy of two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) by leveraging the embedding of their symmetry algebras into the Euler-Arnold Lie algebra of polynomial vector fields. This approach yields a measure of CFT intricacy that surpasses existing metrics, such as the number of operators at a specific dimension and the central charge. We demonstrate that this new measure aligns with the intricacy of the associated Virasoro symmetry algebra and correlates with the intricacy of the corresponding rational CFTs. Furthermore, we establish that the intricacy of any rational CFT is bounded by the degree of its diagonal extension. As a consequence, we prove that the diagonal extension of the $A_{p-1}$ Wess-Zumino-Witten model possesses an intricacy of $p-1$. Finally, we show that the intricacy of rational CFTs increases with the complexity of their character formulas. These findings suggest that the intricacy of a CFT serves as a valuable indicator of the complexity of its character formula. This study presents a forecast regarding the quantity of additional baryons and mesons required to align the cosmic baryon fraction with the baryon content observed in galaxies and the intergalactic medium. The analysis utilizes a Bayesian framework to integrate baryon fraction measurements from the cosmic microwave background with data on baryons within galaxies and the intergalactic medium. The results indicate that the baryon fraction in galaxies and the intergalactic medium is likely underrepresented by a factor of 1.1 to 1.2, with a 95% credible range of 0.9 to 1.3. Consequently, the existence of extra baryons is unlikely, as the 95% credible interval for the ratio of observed to expected baryon fractions in galaxies and the intergalactic medium exceeds 0.9. These findings suggest that the missing baryons are not concentrated in a single, easily identifiable component. Instead, they are probably distributed across numerous small, diffuse structures that remain undetected by current observational methods. The Bayesian framework employed in this work is detailed in Section 2, while the data sources and their corresponding models are described in Section 3. The results are discussed in Section 4, and the conclusions are summarized in Section 5. The data and code utilized for this analysis are accessible at https://github.com/AdrianBuckley/BaryonFraction.

This work introduces SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM counterparts for the title of our paper: Wideband Waveforming for Integrated Data and Energy Delivery: Creating Extra Gain Beyond Multiple Antennas and Multiple Carriers. We formulate the joint data and energy rate maximization problem for both systems under per-user data rate, total power, and peak power constraints. By decomposing the wideband scenario into narrowband subchannels, we derive the optimal solution for the single-user MISO-OFDM system. For the SISO-OFDM system, we propose a low-complexity algorithm that achieves near-optimal performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the wideband waveforming approach significantly outperforms the narrowband multi-carrier method in terms of data rate. Furthermore, the performance gains from wideband waveforming increase with the number of antennas and the bandwidth. These findings confirm that wideband waveforming offers substantial benefits for integrated data and energy delivery systems. Fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) to experimental data is a non-linear inverse problem that requires a Bayesian approach to derive a posteriori probability distributions. This process involves two main stages: first, constructing a likelihood function from data and a prior from theoretical assumptions to form an unnormalized posterior; and second, normalizing this posterior to extract the final PDF. While the first stage is well-established, the second has historically relied on Monte Carlo integration, which is computationally expensive and difficult to scale. This paper introduces a novel method for normalizing the posterior using a deterministic integration technique called the theory framework. We demonstrate that this approach is more efficient than Monte Carlo methods and can be easily scaled to large datasets. Furthermore, we show that the theory framework can be integrated with neural networks to create a fast, differentiable, and accurate PDF fitting framework. We validate this new method by fitting the NNPDF3.1 dataset, which includes 1,000 data points, and the larger NNPDF4.0 dataset, which contains 10,000 points. The results confirm that the theory framework is both efficient and accurate, with the NNPDF4.0 fit requiring approximately 100 times fewer function evaluations than the Monte Carlo method. Additionally, we find that the theory framework is more accurate than the Monte Carlo approach, particularly in the high-$x$ region. Finally, we present a new set of PDFs, named NNPDF4.0-FW, derived using the theory framework. These results indicate that the theory framework is a powerful tool for normalizing the posterior in PDF fitting, offering significant advantages in both efficiency and accuracy. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/NNPDF/tf.

This study introduces a linearized model of a turbulent jet flame's response to acoustic forcing, grounded in an active flame framework. The model incorporates linearized boundary conditions at the inlet and outlet, along with a linearized coupling between the acoustic field and the flame. To validate this approach, the linearized boundary conditions were compared against those derived from a linearized Euler model, demonstrating strong agreement. Furthermore, the model's predictions were verified by comparing them with linearized results from a large-eddy simulation. The findings confirm that the linearized active flame model accurately captures the flame's response to acoustic forcing. Additionally, the model was employed to investigate the flame's response to a combination of inlet velocity and pressure acoustic modes. The results indicate that the flame's response to inlet velocity fluctuations is significantly more pronounced than its response to pressure fluctuations. Finally, the model was used to examine how the flame reacts to acoustic modes with varying frequencies and wavenumbers, revealing that the response to velocity fluctuations is most intense when the acoustic wavelength aligns with the flame's length. These results suggest that the linearized active flame model serves as a valuable tool for analyzing the response of turbulent jet flames to acoustic forcing. Nonlocal gravity, a theory grounded in the principle of locality within a nonlocal spacetime, offers a compelling framework for addressing the cosmological constant problem. This approach posits that gravity arises from nonlocal interactions between matter and spacetime, mediated by a nonlocal field. In this work, we introduce a constitutive relation for nonlocal gravity, detailing how nonlocal gravitational effects emerge from nonlocal spacetime interactions. We also examine the connection between nonlocal gravity and the Einstein-Ardron theory. Furthermore, we define a fundamental frame for nonlocal gravity, analogous to the fundamental frames in nonlocal electrodynamics and elasticity, and derive the corresponding constitutive relation for nonlocal gravity within this fundamental frame. Finally, we demonstrate that the nonlocal gravitational effects observed in a general frame result from nonlocal interactions between the nonlocal gravitational field and the fundamental frame. These findings provide a comprehensive description of nonlocal gravitational phenomena across arbitrary frames. The constitutive relation for nonlocal gravity in the fundamental frame is derived in Appendix A, while the derivation of nonlocal gravitational effects in a general frame is detailed in Appendix B. This study extends the constitutive approach to nonlocal gravity, a field that has not yet been fully explored. The introduction of a constitutive relation for nonlocal gravity in the fundamental frame enables the formulation of nonlocal gravitational effects in any frame, thereby offering a complete description of these phenomena. Additionally, this constitutive relation serves as a foundation for deriving the equations of motion for nonlocal gravity. The concept of a fundamental frame for nonlocal gravity is also significant for investigating nonlocal gravitational anomalies. By defining a constitutive relation for nonlocal gravity in the fundamental frame, we can derive the equations of motion for nonlocal gravitational effects in any frame, including the fundamental frame itself. This allows for the identification of nonlocal gravitational anomalies in the fundamental frame, which may be linked to the cosmological constant problem. Ultimately, the constitutive relation for nonlocal gravity in the fundamental frame acts as a crucial tool for exploring nonlocal gravitational anomalies. Neutron star X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre have long been hypothesized to be in a transient state, characterized by periodic outbursts followed by quiescent phases. This study examines the recurrence intervals of transient events in nine confirmed neutron star X-ray binaries within the Galactic Centre. The analysis reveals that these intervals follow a power-law distribution with a slope of $\alpha=1.7\pm0.1$, a finding that aligns with the self-organized criticality model. This model posits that accretion-driven outbursts result from the global synchronization of magnetic field line reconnection events occurring at the neutron star's surface. Furthermore, the data indicate that the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are likely in a transient state, with recurrence intervals ranging from 10 to 100 years. Consequently, the absence of observed outbursts from these systems over the past few decades is consistent with their transient nature. These results suggest that the quiescent neutron star X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are transient systems with recurrence intervals between 10 and 100 years, rather than persistent ones. This conclusion carries significant implications for the prospects of detecting gravitational wave signals from neutron star mergers in the Galactic Centre. Additionally, the study proposes that the recurrence interval of a transient neutron star X-ray binary is inversely proportional to the square of its mass accretion rate. This relationship implies that the transient systems in the Galactic Centre have lower mass accretion rates compared to the transient neutron star X-ray binaries found in the Milky Way's disk. Finally, the research suggests that the transient systems in the Galactic Centre are unlikely to be in a low-hard state, as this state typically requires higher mass accretion rates. Instead, they are likely in a low-soft state, which is characterized by a lower mass accretion rate and a thermal-dominated spectrum. These findings offer new insights into the nature of the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre and the physical mechanisms governing the recurrence intervals of transient events in neutron star X-ray binaries. The analysis of recurrence intervals also provides a method for estimating the mass accretion rates of transient systems in the Galactic Centre, which can help identify the origins of their accreting material. Ultimately, this study presents a novel approach for determining mass accretion rates in transient neutron star X-ray binaries. Bipartite graphs serve as a fundamental model for numerous real-world scenarios, including social networks, biological systems, and information retrieval. A central challenge in this domain is the bipartite vertex splitting problem, which involves converting a general graph into a bipartite one by splitting its vertices. This task is significant because it enables the application of specialized algorithms designed for bipartite graphs to general graphs. However, existing methods for solving this problem are either computationally expensive or limited to specific graph types. This paper introduces a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm for the bipartite vertex splitting problem, offering a more efficient solution than current approaches. We validate the effectiveness of our algorithm through extensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques, particularly for graphs with high degrees of non-bipartiteness. Furthermore, we provide a complete characterization of the parameter for which the problem is fixed-parameter tractable. These findings suggest that the proposed algorithm can effectively address the bipartite vertex splitting problem for a broader range of graphs than previously possible. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/BVS-FPT.

This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel technique designed to extend the operational lifespan of CPUs by reducing their clock frequency. Unlike conventional methods that lower frequency uniformly across all cores, HyperDegrade selectively decreases the frequency of specific cores based on their current workload. This targeted approach allows for greater frequency reductions without compromising overall system performance. The method operates by dynamically adjusting the frequency of individual cores in response to workload variations, ensuring that performance remains stable even when the total system frequency is significantly lowered. To achieve this, HyperDegrade employs a lightweight, online learning algorithm that continuously monitors workload changes and optimizes core frequencies accordingly. Experimental results demonstrate that HyperDegrade can reduce CPU frequency by up to 75% while maintaining performance levels comparable to those of a system running at full speed. These findings indicate that HyperDegrade offers a viable solution for prolonging CPU longevity, particularly in scenarios where performance degradation is acceptable. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to a wide range of CPU models, including those with up to 64 cores. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation for classical and welded links, termed the "new crossing change" (NCC). We demonstrate that the NCC is a composition of two previously established unknotting operations: the crossing change and the detour move. Furthermore, we establish that the NCC is a local unknotting operation for both classical and welded links, and we derive a formula for the minimal number of NCCs required to unknot a classical or welded link. As applications, we prove that the unknotting number and the new unknotting number via NCC are equivalent for classical and welded torus knots. Additionally, we show that the new unknotting number via NCC is equivalent to the sum of the unknotting number and the writhe for classical and welded pretzel knots. Finally, we provide a formula for the minimal number of NCCs needed to transform a classical or welded link into a trivial link with a specified writhe. These results offer a fresh perspective on unknotting numbers and related unknotting operations for classical and welded links. The new unknotting operation via NCC may also have significant applications in knot theory, particularly in the study of knot invariants and the classification of knots. This study tackles the problem of synchronizing the phases of $N$ oscillators distributed across a regular network, where each node operates under limited computational and communication constraints. We introduce a novel, fully distributed algorithm that leverages a multi-task framework to achieve synchronization. The proposed method relies on a simple, low-complexity protocol requiring only local phase measurements and the exchange of a single integer per time step. We establish that, for a specific class of regular graphs, the algorithm guarantees asymptotic synchronization. Furthermore, we derive an explicit upper bound on the convergence rate, demonstrating that the convergence speed increases with the number of tasks. Numerical simulations are provided to validate the theoretical findings and illustrate the algorithm's performance. The results indicate that the convergence rate can be significantly accelerated by increasing the number of tasks, provided the network topology supports it. Additionally, the simulations reveal that the algorithm remains effective even when the number of tasks exceeds the node degree, a scenario where traditional methods fail. These outcomes suggest that the proposed approach offers a viable solution for synchronizing large-scale networks of oscillators with limited resources. The algorithm is applicable to various systems, including robotic networks, sensor networks, and biological networks. The core concept of multi-task synchronization is detailed in Section II, while the specific algorithm for synchronizing $N$ oscillators over a regular graph is presented in Section III. Simulation results are discussed in Section IV, and the paper concludes in Section V.

The sensitivity of current gravitational wave detectors at high frequencies is constrained by shot noise, a limitation that will persist even with planned upgrades to future detectors. To address this, we propose a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, a novel configuration that leverages the unique characteristics of a Sagnac interferometer to enhance high-frequency sensitivity. By integrating this design with a power-recycled Michelson interferometer, we create a hybrid sloshing-Sagnac Michelson interferometer. Our analysis indicates that this configuration could achieve a 1.5 dB improvement in high-frequency sensitivity compared to a conventional Michelson interferometer. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sloshing-Sagnac setup can be implemented using existing detector components, such as beam splitters and mirrors, without requiring additional optical elements. Finally, we confirm that the sloshing-Sagnac Michelson interferometer maintains the same signal response as a standard Michelson interferometer. These findings suggest that the sloshing-Sagnac Michelson design is a viable solution for improving high-frequency sensitivity in current and future gravitational wave detectors. Although neural language models have largely superseded $n$-gram models in recent years, we demonstrate that integrating $n$-gram features into neural architectures yields further performance gains. Specifically, we introduce a residual learning framework for neural text generation that leverages $n$-gram language models as auxiliary components. Our approach, termed $N$-gram+Neural, utilizes a neural sequence-to-sequence model to predict the residuals between an $n$-gram model's scores and the actual data distribution. We validate this method on two tasks: neural machine translation and abstractive summarization. Our findings indicate that $N$-gram+Neural outperforms standard neural models, achieving a 0.2 BLEU point improvement in machine translation and a 0.1 ROUGE point gain in summarization. Furthermore, we observe that the benefits of incorporating $n$-gram features increase with the size of the neural model's vocabulary. To address the high memory requirements of large $n$-gram models, we propose a novel data structure that enables the use of 100-gram models with a vocabulary of 100,000 words, requiring only 1.5 GB of memory. Finally, we confirm that $N$-gram+Neural also surpasses existing residual models that rely on $k$-nearest neighbor and $k$-backoff language models. The source code for this work is available at: https://github.com/IBM/ngram-plus-neural.

This study introduces iOCR, an informed end-to-end neural network designed to identify the specific OCR model responsible for generating the most accurate character recognition for each individual text region on a ballot image. By leveraging a large dataset of 1.5 million image-text pairs derived from 100,000 ballots across 10 states, we trained a suite of 11 distinct OCR models. These models were evaluated on 100,000 test ballots from 10 states, with performance measured using the Levenshtein distance between the predicted and actual text. The resulting dataset, comprising 1.5 million records of ballot images, corresponding text regions, and their associated Levenshtein distances, is publicly available at https://github.com/PrincetonUniversityX/iOCR. Our findings indicate that a single OCR model is insufficient for all ballots; rather, the optimal model varies depending on the image region, ballot type, and state. Consequently, an informed approach that selects the best-performing OCR model for each region yields a 10% reduction in Levenshtein distance compared to using a single model. Furthermore, this informed method outperforms a baseline that combines Tesseract with a post-processing dictionary of 10,000 state-specific words by 15%. The iOCR system is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/PrincetonUniversityX/iOCR. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that an end-to-end neural network can surpass the performance of a neural network paired with a post-processing dictionary, offering a promising direction for future research. Additionally, the proposed framework is adaptable to other domains where multiple models are available for a specific task, such as medical imaging, where different models may excel at identifying various types of anomalies.

This study examines the atmospheric circulation patterns of terrestrial planets within simplified global circulation models (GCMs). The model incorporates a simplified radiative-convective equilibrium, a shallow cumulus convection parameterization, and a frictionless, inviscid atmosphere. We find that the circulation structure is primarily determined by the ratio of planetary rotation rate to the convective turnover time. For rapidly rotating planets, the atmosphere exhibits a baroclinic instability characterized by eddy-driven jets and storm tracks, similar to Earth. In contrast, slowly rotating planets develop a cyclostrophic circulation with a strong equatorial super-rotating jet and a weak poleward flow, resembling the atmospheres of Venus and Titan. A transition between these two regimes occurs at a critical rotation rate, where the circulation shifts from cyclostrophic to baroclinic. At this critical point, the atmosphere becomes unstable to barotropic instabilities, manifesting as Rossby wave instabilities and Kelvin waves. These instabilities generate eddies that facilitate angular momentum transport, driving the super-rotating jet. This mechanism aligns with recent findings from 3D GCMs and observations of tidally locked exoplanets, suggesting that a similar process may occur on slowly rotating terrestrial planets. Additionally, we observe that the atmosphere of a slowly rotating planet with a high obliquity (90°) develops a circulation pattern akin to that of a rapidly rotating planet with a low obliquity (23.5°). This suggests that the circulation of slowly rotating planets is more influenced by the Rossby number than by the obliquity angle. These results offer insights into the atmospheric circulation of terrestrial planets, including those with extreme rotation rates or obliquities, such as tidally locked exoplanets and super-Earths. Furthermore, these findings provide a framework for understanding the atmospheric circulation of terrestrial planets in simplified GCMs and may aid in interpreting the circulation patterns of Earth-like planets in 3D GCMs. The detailed circulation structures identified in this work can also serve as a foundation for investigating atmospheric thermal structures and cloud formation in GCMs. Ultimately, these results may assist in interpreting the atmospheric circulation of terrestrial planets observed by future atmospheric sounding missions. This paper is the first of two; the second part will explore the thermal structures and cloud formation of terrestrial planets in simplified GCMs.

We introduce a stochastic hydrodynamic framework for interacting Bose gases formulated within the positive-P phase-space representation. This approach integrates the hydrodynamic equations for an ideal Bose gas with a stochastic noise term derived from the positive-P representation to account for interactions. The resulting model, termed the positive-P random quantum hydrodynamic (PRQH) framework, is validated by demonstrating that the single-particle Wigner function aligns with the Bogoliubov approximation for weakly interacting systems. Furthermore, we show that the PRQH framework accurately reproduces the single-particle correlation function and two-particle density matrix for a Bose gas confined in a harmonic trap, even under strong interaction conditions. Finally, we apply this framework to investigate the dynamics of a Bose gas following a sudden change in trap frequency, finding that the single-particle correlation function exhibits oscillations arising from the interference of Bogoliubov modes. These oscillations persist until the system reaches a thermalized state, at which point the correlation function decays to a constant value. The PRQH framework offers a practical method for simulating the dynamics of interacting Bose gases, potentially enabling the study of phenomena such as superfluidity and vortex formation. The code used for these simulations is available at https://github.com/AdityaGupta1997/PRQH.

This paper surveys the Instructor-Student architecture, a framework designed to enhance knowledge learning in neural networks. In this model, an "instructor" network generates predictions for unlabeled data, which are then used to train a "student" network. The instructor is subsequently updated using the student's predictions on unlabeled data. This iterative process continues until the student achieves satisfactory performance on the target task. We examine the evolution of this architecture, detailing its applications in knowledge distillation, domain adaptation, and multi-task learning. Furthermore, we analyze the associated theoretical challenges and propose potential solutions. Finally, we outline future research directions for this framework. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the Instructor-Student architecture and its various applications. The corresponding GitHub repository is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi-001/Instructor-Student-Architecture-for-Knowledge-Learning-A-Survey.

This study introduces a novel exact test designed to evaluate the performance of structured test statistics within the paired-permutation framework. The proposed method, termed the precise paired-permutation test, offers a more accurate approach for assessing structured test statistics in the context of paired-permutation testing. We demonstrate that the precise paired-permutation test yields a more accurate p-value than the conventional paired-permutation test. Furthermore, we establish that the precise paired-permutation test maintains exact size control under the null hypothesis. To validate these findings, we conducted a simulation study and applied the test to real-world data. The results indicate that the precise paired-permutation test produces a more accurate p-value compared to the standard paired-permutation test. Additionally, the simulation study reveals that the conventional paired-permutation test may fail to maintain the correct size under the null hypothesis, whereas the precise version ensures exact size control. Finally, we provide R code to implement the precise paired-permutation test for various structured test statistics, including the t-test, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and F-test. This work represents the first attempt to develop a precise paired-permutation test for structured test statistics. The proposed method can be integrated into other research areas, such as bioinformatics, to enhance the accuracy of p-values in paired-permutation testing. Ultimately, this advancement contributes to the development of more reliable statistical tests for bioinformatics applications. The precise paired-permutation test is particularly valuable for scenarios where the p-value from a paired-permutation test is close to the significance level, as it delivers a more accurate result. For instance, in bioinformatics, when determining whether a gene is differentially expressed, a more precise p-value is essential for making informed decisions. We anticipate that this method will be adopted in future research to improve the accuracy of p-values in paired-permutation testing. Furthermore, the $v_3$ coefficient exhibits a stronger dependence on centrality in Cu+Cu collisions compared to Au+Au collisions, a trend that mirrors the experimental observations. This paper introduces a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that incorporates a partially grid-based origin model, designed for tracking multiple targets within a bounded area. The proposed PMBM filter with a partially grid-based origin model (PMBM-PO) integrates a point process for the Poisson component and a hybrid representation for the Bernoulli component, which combines a grid-based probability mass function (PMF) with a Gaussian distribution. To implement this filter, we first derive a PMF-based origin model using a grid and a corresponding PMF. Subsequently, we develop a hybrid origin model by merging this PMF-based model with a Gaussian distribution. Finally, we formulate the prediction and update steps for the PMBM-PO filter. Simulation results demonstrate that the PMBM-PO filter effectively estimates the number of targets and their locations. Furthermore, these simulations validate the effectiveness of a sensor management strategy based on the PMBM-PO filter for optimizing sensor trajectories. The findings indicate that the sensor management approach utilizing the PMBM-PO filter outperforms the standard PMBM filter in terms of root mean square error (RMSE) for target number estimation and achieves higher detection probabilities. This confirms that the partially grid-based origin model enhances the accuracy of target number estimation. The proposed PMBM-PO filter and its associated sensor management strategy are applicable to scenarios involving multiple sensors and targets, such as air defense, surveillance, and search and rescue operations. Soccer represents a dynamic, multi-agent, and partially observable environment, making it an ideal candidate for applying deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to enhance player performance. While numerous studies have explored this area, most have concentrated on optimizing a single action, such as shooting, to increase goal-scoring chances. However, in real-world soccer, players must select the most effective action for each specific situation. This paper introduces a novel framework that leverages a multi-task learning approach to simultaneously learn and optimize multiple actions within a given context. We propose a new state representation and a multi-task learning architecture designed to improve the selection of optimal actions in critical game moments. Our method utilizes a combination of a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a recurrent neural network (RNN) to process the proposed state representation. To evaluate our approach, we employed a soccer dataset comprising 1,000 games from the 2017/2018 and 2018/2019 seasons of the Italian Serie A. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of both accuracy and F1-score. Furthermore, we conducted a detailed analysis of the optimal actions learned by our model, offering insights into its decision-making process. The source code for this work is available at: https://github.com/ahmadreza99/EnhancedActions.

Laser Doppler vibrometry (LDV) is a non-contact optical technique capable of precisely measuring vibration velocities at specific points on structures. While single-point LDV systems are limited to capturing data at one location, multi-point configurations are required to obtain 2D or 3D vibration information. This study introduces a method to generate 2D measurements using a single-point LDV system through a combination of optical and digital image processing. The approach involves creating a virtual multi-point system by directing the laser beam to multiple points on the structure via a mirror array. The resulting Doppler signals from these points are then processed using digital image processing to reconstruct the 2D vibration velocity distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that this method enables the acquisition of 2D vibration velocity data from a single-point LDV system at a distance of 10 meters. These findings suggest that this technique can be applied to monitor the vibration velocity distribution of large structures, such as wind turbine blades, without requiring complex multi-point LDV setups. Additionally, the method offers a cost-effective solution for obtaining 2D vibration velocity data using a single-point LDV system. The proposed technique is particularly valuable for scenarios involving large structures where installing multiple LDV sensors is impractical or where the use of a single LDV system is preferred for cost and maintenance reasons. Ultimately, this approach facilitates the remote operation of a single-point LDV system to capture 2D vibration velocity data from large structures, providing a viable alternative to traditional multi-point LDV configurations. The method is detailed in Section 2, with experimental results presented in Section 3, followed by conclusions in Section 4.

This study introduces a Monte Carlo approach to simulate the time evolution of a quantum harmonic oscillator under a constant force, a system that lacks a straightforward analytical solution. By employing a discrete time path integral formulation, we developed a Monte Carlo algorithm to numerically calculate the system's time evolution operator. The results demonstrate that the Monte Carlo method yields accurate outcomes, aligning closely with the exact analytical solution for the undriven quantum harmonic oscillator. Furthermore, the Monte Carlo simulation successfully reproduces the expected time evolution for the driven system. These findings confirm that Monte Carlo techniques can effectively simulate the time evolution of quantum systems, offering a viable alternative to analytical methods. This approach is particularly valuable for systems where analytical solutions are unattainable, such as those with complex potentials or interactions. The proposed Monte Carlo algorithm is generalizable to any quantum system described by a path integral formulation. Additionally, this work provides a pedagogical example of how Monte Carlo methods can be applied to simulate quantum systems, potentially serving as a useful resource for students and researchers in the field. Vector magnetograms are essential for forecasting solar eruptions and are crucial for validating data-driven models in solar physics. These instruments rely on the Zeeman effect to infer magnetic field vectors from spectral line profiles. However, this inference process is ill-posed, meaning that multiple magnetic field configurations can produce identical line profiles. Consequently, the resulting measurements are inherently biased and represent only an approximation of the actual field. This study introduces a novel method to identify and mitigate these biases in inferred vector magnetic field data. We demonstrate that the bias stems from the specific line profile fitting algorithm used to derive the measurements. By decoupling the fitting algorithm from the data acquisition process, we show that the bias can be eliminated. Our approach involves creating a new dataset of vector magnetic fields using a different fitting algorithm, which we then compare against the original measurements to quantify the bias. We apply this methodology to a dataset of solar active region 12673, originally collected by the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). Our results indicate that the bias in the HMI vector magnetic field measurements is significant, particularly in areas where the magnetic field is strong and inclined. Furthermore, we find that the bias in the HMI's inferred line-of-sight magnetic field component is substantial, even in regions where the field is weak. Finally, we present a corrected dataset of vector magnetic fields for active region 12673, derived from the original HMI data by removing the identified bias. This corrected dataset is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1094000. These findings suggest that the bias in HMI vector magnetic field measurements is likely a widespread issue affecting all solar vector magnetogram datasets. We conclude by discussing the implications of these results for solar physics research and space weather forecasting. The new dataset of corrected vector magnetic fields for active region 12673 is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1094000. This study investigates how different loss functions influence the performance of deep learning models used for classification tasks. We evaluated five specific loss functions: Cross Entropy, Focal, Tversky, Generalized Focal, and Generalized Tversky. The assessment was conducted using two datasets: the MNIST handwritten digit dataset and the PASCAL VOC 2007 dataset, which contains images of 20 distinct object categories. Our results indicate that the Focal loss function yields the best outcomes for the MNIST dataset, while the Generalized Tversky loss performs optimally for the PASCAL VOC 2007 dataset. Furthermore, we observed that the Generalized Focal loss function delivers superior results compared to the standard Focal loss when applied to the PASCAL VOC 2007 dataset. These findings suggest that selecting an appropriate loss function is crucial for enhancing classification performance. Additionally, we determined that the Generalized Tversky loss function is particularly effective for datasets characterized by significant class imbalance. To support these conclusions, we provide a detailed analysis of the results and include a comparative evaluation of the five loss functions. Video prediction remains a significant challenge in computer vision, primarily due to the difficulty of modeling temporal dynamics. This paper introduces a novel framework for predicting new view videos by leveraging a dual representation. First, we convert new view videos into a latent space using an encoder trained on existing new view data. Second, we forecast the latent representation of the new view video by integrating the latent representation of the corresponding old view video with its future trajectory. Finally, we reconstruct the predicted new view video from the forecasted latent representation. To address the scarcity of new view data, we propose a two-stage training approach: initially, we train the encoder and predictor on old view videos, and subsequently, we train both components on new view videos. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in predicting new view videos. The metric dimension of a graph $G$, denoted by $\beta(G)$, represents the minimum cardinality of a resolving set for $G$. This concept has been extensively studied due to its significance in applications such as network de-centralized localization, chemical structure identification, and robotics. In this paper, we introduce a new parameter called the trimmed metric dimension, defined as the smallest cardinality of a subset $S$ of vertices such that $G$ admits a resolving set within the union of $S$ and its $r$-neighbourhood. We denote this parameter by $\beta_r(G)$. We establish that for any tree $T$ with $n$ vertices, $\beta_r(T) \leq \lceil n/2 \rceil$, and we characterize the trees for which equality holds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and diameter $d$, $\beta_r(G) \leq n - d + 1$. We also determine the exact value of $\beta_r(G)$ for several specific graph families. Additionally, we prove that for any integers $n$ and $r$ satisfying $n \geq 2r+1$, there exists a graph with $n$ vertices and diameter $2r$ for which $\beta_r(G) = n - r$. Finally, we show that for any integers $n$ and $k$ with $n \geq 2k+1$, there exists a graph with $n$ vertices and diameter $2k$ such that $\beta_k(G) = n - k + 1$. These results indicate that the trimmed metric dimension can be significantly smaller than the standard metric dimension. We conclude by outlining several open problems related to this parameter. This study examines the subthermal excitation of C{\sc i} spectral lines within the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies. We analyzed 12 galaxies from the ALFALFA survey that possess both 21\,cm and CO data, utilizing a Bayesian framework to derive the best-fit parameters for a two-level model. Our findings indicate that the C{\sc i} lines in these galaxies are indeed subthermally excited, with an average excitation temperature of $T_{\rm ex}=2.7\pm0.1$\,K. This value aligns closely with the cosmic microwave background temperature ($T_{\rm cmb}=2.725$\,K), suggesting that the C{\sc i} emission in these galaxies is primarily driven by cosmic rays rather than collisions. Consequently, the 21\,cm and CO luminosities serve as more reliable indicators of the total gas mass ($M_{\rm tot}$) than the C{\sc i} luminosity. We also investigated the relationship between $M_{\rm tot}$ and the star formation rate (SFR), observing a significant flattening of the SFR--$M_{\rm tot}$ relation at high gas masses when using the C{\sc i} luminosity as the tracer. This flattening is likely an artifact caused by the underestimation of $M_{\rm tot}$ due to subthermal excitation. Furthermore, we explored the connection between $M_{\rm tot}$ and the specific star formation rate (sSFR), confirming that galaxies with $M_{\rm tot}>10^{9.5}\,M_{\odot}$ exhibit lower sSFRs. Finally, we demonstrated that the ratio of 21\,cm to CO luminosity can function as a tracer for the gas-phase metallicity ($Z_{\rm gas}$), with a correlation coefficient of $r=0.57$. This ratio offers a valuable tool for estimating $Z_{\rm gas}$ in galaxies where CO data are unavailable. Overall, this work highlights the significance of the subthermal excitation of C{\sc i} lines in galaxies and underscores the utility of the 21\,cm to CO luminosity ratio as a proxy for gas-phase metallicity. These insights are crucial for interpreting the chemical evolution of galaxies and the origin of their molecular gas reservoirs. We introduce and examine the velocity process associated with the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) on a finite lattice, a concept originally proposed by Ferrari and co-authors in 1996. This process tracks the time evolution of particle currents across the lattice sites. We establish that, when the system starts from a Bernoulli product measure, the velocity process is Markovian and converges to a specific diffusion process as the lattice size approaches infinity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the invariant measure for this limiting diffusion is a mixture of Poisson distributions. Finally, we provide a detailed description of the stationary distribution for the ASEP velocity process on a finite lattice, which is characterized as a mixture of independent Poisson distributions. This characterization is derived using a novel representation of the ASEP that incorporates a random environment. As a consequence, we offer a new proof of the product structure of the invariant measure for the ASEP, a result originally established by Liggett in 1977. Additionally, we show that the invariant measure for the velocity process on a finite lattice is a mixture of product measures, a finding that may have broader applications. These results are significant for understanding the hydrodynamic limit of the ASEP and for analyzing the behavior of the process under non-product initial conditions. The detailed characterization of the invariant measure for the velocity process on a finite lattice also holds potential value for studying the convergence of the ASEP to its hydrodynamic limit. To achieve these findings, we develop a new representation of the ASEP that incorporates a random environment. This representation may be useful for addressing other problems related to the ASEP. The correlation between galaxies' stellar mass ($M_*$) and star formation rate (SFR), known as the $M_*$-SFR relation, exhibits a downturn at high $M_*$. While gas supply and consumption have traditionally been viewed as the primary drivers of this turnover, recent findings suggest that active galactic nuclei (AGN) also play a significant role. This study utilizes a suite of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations to investigate the relative contributions of gas supply, consumption, and AGN feedback to the $M_*$-SFR downturn. Our results indicate that gas supply and consumption are the dominant factors, whereas the impact of AGN feedback is minor. Specifically, the downturn arises because gas supply declines more rapidly than consumption at high $M_*$. We attribute this to a reduction in cold gas accretion from the circumgalactic medium (CGM) onto the galaxy disk, driven by the suppression of CGM cooling by hot gas. This suppression occurs because, at high $M_*$, the heating from supernovae and stellar feedback is insufficient to offset radiative cooling, leading to an overabundance of cold gas in the CGM. Consequently, this excess cold gas is retained in the CGM rather than accreting onto the disk. We conclude that the $M_*$-SFR downturn is fundamentally caused by the inability of galaxies to accrete sufficient cold gas from the CGM to fuel star formation, a process regulated by the thermal balance between heating and cooling in the CGM. These insights offer a new perspective on the physical mechanisms governing the $M_*$-SFR relation and the evolution of galaxy star formation. We report the detection of a rapid spin-up phase in the low-mass X-ray binary 4U 1608-52, where the neutron star's rotation accelerated from approximately 10 Hz to 14 Hz over a period of roughly 100 days. This acceleration corresponds to an accretion torque of $1.2 \times 10^{30}$ dyne cm, which is roughly twice the torque required to maintain the current 14 Hz spin. This finding indicates that the torque exerted by the inner edge of the accretion disk on the neutron star is significantly stronger than the torque generated by magnetic braking at the outer edge of the disk. Consequently, the system is likely undergoing a spin-up instability, a phenomenon previously observed in only a handful of low-mass X-ray binaries. The torque balance between magnetic braking and accretion torque, combined with the measured mass accretion rate, suggests that the inner disk edge is located at a radius of 1.5--2 times the neutron star's radius. This implies that the neutron star is either accreting from a disk that has been pushed to its surface by the consumption of a low-mass companion, or that angular momentum transport within the disk is more efficient than standard $\alpha$-disk models predict. These results provide compelling evidence for either the consumption of a low-mass companion or enhanced angular momentum transport in the disk, both of which are essential for explaining the existence of millisecond pulsars. Furthermore, the observed spin-up instability offers a potential method for detecting the consumption of low-mass companions. The rapid spin-up of 4U 1608-52 also suggests that the previously hypothesized "spin-up instability" in high-mass X-ray binaries may be a misinterpretation of this spin-up instability occurring in a low-mass companion. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the formation of millisecond pulsars. These conclusions are derived from a detailed analysis of the X-ray and optical light curves, as well as the X-ray spectrum, of 4U 1608-52. The optical light curve was measured using the 1.8-m Tzec Maun telescope at the Center for High Performance Astrophysics (CHiPA) at the University of North Dakota, while the X-ray light curve and spectrum were obtained with the NICER instrument on board the ISS. Golay complementary arrays (GCAs) are a specific type of Golay sequence pair composed of array sequences, which have garnered significant attention due to their potential applications in radar systems and wireless communications. This paper introduces a novel construction method for GCA matrices with lengths $N=4p^{\alpha}q^{\beta}$, where $p$ and $q$ are distinct primes, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are positive integers, and $N$ is a multiple of 4. The proposed construction utilizes a combination of Golay complementary sequences, GCA matrices, and a new class of GCA matrices derived from Golay complementary array sequences. Furthermore, we present a construction for GCA matrices with length $N=4p^{\alpha}q^{\beta}r^{\gamma}$, where $r$ is a prime distinct from $p$ and $q$, and $\gamma$ is a positive integer. Finally, we establish a general construction for GCA matrices with length $N=4N_1N_2$, where $N_1$ and $N_2$ are positive integers. These constructions are grounded in the concatenation of Golay complementary array sequences and GCA matrices. The resulting GCA matrices with length $N=4p^{\alpha}q^{\beta}r^{\gamma}$ are termed $4p^{\alpha}q^{\beta}r^{\gamma}$-order GCA matrices, while those with length $N=4N_1N_2$ are referred to as $4N_1N_2$-order GCA matrices. We also introduce a construction for GCA matrices with length $N=4p^{\alpha}q^{\beta}r^{\gamma}N_1N_2$, called $4p^{\alpha}q^{\beta}r^{\gamma}N_1N_2$-order GCA matrices. Brain injuries represent a significant global health challenge, yet the scarcity of annotated data hinders the development of effective deep learning models for brain injury detection. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework for synthesizing brain injury images using a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVAE). This approach integrates a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) with a Progressive GAN to generate high-quality brain injury images. The model operates in two stages: initially, a VAE learns the latent distribution of brain images to produce synthetic normal brain images; subsequently, a Progressive GAN refines these outputs to create realistic brain injury images. Experimental results demonstrate that the synthesized images achieve a Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) of 1.99, surpassing existing methods. Furthermore, the model effectively learns the latent distribution of brain injury images, enabling the generation of diverse injury types. These findings confirm that the proposed PAVAE framework can produce high-quality synthetic brain injury images, offering a valuable resource for training deep learning models in brain injury detection. Feature extraction serves as a fundamental component in numerous computer vision tasks, including image classification, detection, and segmentation. While various methods exist, they often lack a unified framework. This paper introduces a unified structure for feature extraction grounded in contrastive learning. We first formulate a contrastive learning framework for image classification, demonstrating that the resulting feature space aligns with the optimal solution for classification. Building on this, we propose a unified architecture for feature extraction applicable to multiple vision tasks. We validate the effectiveness of our unified structure across several tasks, including classification, detection, and segmentation. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach for zero-shot image classification, which achieves state-of-the-art performance. This study examines the connection between the first law of black hole thermodynamics and the Euclidean action within the framework of non-linear charged AdS black holes. Quantum entanglement and synchronization represent two distinct non-classical phenomena that have garnered significant attention in recent years. This study examines the interplay between entanglement and synchronization within the Wigner-Weyl-Wick (WWW) framework, utilizing the WWW tomogram as the primary analytical tool. We demonstrate that entanglement and synchronization manifest as specific alterations in the WWW tomogram. Furthermore, we establish that the transition from an entangled to a separable state, as well as the emergence of synchronization, correspond to singularities in the WWW tomogram. These findings offer a novel perspective on quantum entanglement and synchronization, potentially enabling the development of new methods for detecting and quantifying these phenomena. Additionally, we illustrate that the WWW tomogram serves as a valuable resource for investigating other quantum characteristics, such as nonlocality and quantum steering. The results presented herein are derived exclusively from the WWW tomogram, without relying on the wavefunction or density matrix. Consequently, the approach outlined in this work could be applicable to other quantum systems where the wavefunction or density matrix are difficult to determine. Finally, we anticipate that the methodologies and insights developed here will prove useful for analyzing other quantum features within the WWW framework. The detailed procedures for these investigations are documented in the main text and accompanying appendices.

This phenomenon arises from the stick-slip dynamics of the tape as it separates from the surface. While the acoustic power spectrum of this noise follows a $1/f^\alpha$ pattern, indicating self-affine stick-slip behavior, the underlying temporal structure of the noise remains unclear. The analysis reveals that the acoustic power spectrum displays a two-step power-law behavior, which corresponds to a dual-scale temporal structure in the noise. This structure consists of a sequence of slip events, where each event comprises a rapid burst of acoustic power followed by a period of silence. Furthermore, the duration of these silent intervals follows a power-law distribution, suggesting that the stick-slip dynamics occur across two distinct time scales. These findings suggest that the stick-slip dynamics of the tape are governed by a hierarchical structure. Additionally, the duration of the silent intervals is found to be proportional to the pulling velocity, implying that the characteristic time scale of the stick phase is determined by the velocity. These results align with the predictions of a simple model describing the stick-slip dynamics of a viscoelastic interface. In 1928, K. Menger introduced the concept of an abstract angle space, a structure designed to formalize the notion of angle within metric spaces. He investigated the embeddability of such spaces into Euclidean spaces and posed two significant questions regarding this topic. In 1998, N. J. Cutler and R. S. Freese demonstrated that the embeddability of metric spaces into Euclidean spaces does not guarantee the embeddability of their associated abstract angle spaces into Euclidean ones. Furthermore, they proved that if a metric space $X$ embeds into a Hilbert space and its abstract angle space $\mathcal{A}(X)$ embeds into a Euclidean space, then $X$ itself must embed into a Euclidean space. Consequently, they concluded that the embeddability of abstract angle spaces into Euclidean spaces is a stronger condition than the embeddability of the underlying metric spaces. This result led Cutler and Freese to assert that the two questions originally raised by Menger remain unresolved. In this paper, we provide a positive answer to both questions, thereby resolving the issue of whether the embeddability of metric spaces into Euclidean spaces implies the embeddability of their abstract angle spaces into Euclidean spaces. Our solution relies on a novel characterization of the embeddability of metric spaces into Hilbert spaces, which we establish as a consequence of a new characterization of the embeddability of abstract angle spaces into Euclidean spaces. Additionally, we offer a fresh characterization of the embeddability of metric spaces into Hilbert spaces. These characterizations yield further insights into the embeddability of both metric spaces and their associated abstract angle spaces into Hilbert spaces. Finally, we present a new characterization of the embeddability of metric spaces into Euclidean spaces. As a corollary, we derive a new characterization of the embeddability of abstract angle spaces into Euclidean spaces. These results collectively provide a comprehensive characterization of the embeddability of metric spaces into Hilbert spaces. To achieve these findings, we introduce a new class of spaces termed "generalized abstract angle spaces," which serve as a generalization of the traditional abstract angle spaces. We also establish a new characterization of the embeddability of metric spaces into Euclidean spaces, which may be of independent interest. The primary tools employed in our proofs are the Gram matrix and the Gram operator. We conclude the paper with a list of open problems. Point cloud models have gained traction in computer vision due to their ability to handle unordered 3D data. However, existing models often struggle with generalization, failing to accurately predict unseen point clouds that undergo transformations like rotation, scaling, or translation. This limitation arises because current architectures lack invariance to these transformations. To address this, we introduce a novel regularization method called Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC), which enforces invariance to specific transformations. We validate the effectiveness of TPC across various point cloud models, including PointNet, PointNet++, and DGCNN, demonstrating that it significantly enhances generalization. Our approach is simple, model-agnostic, and requires no additional training data. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset of transformed point clouds to evaluate generalization. Our findings indicate that TPC substantially improves generalization, with accuracy gains of up to 10% on unseen transformed point clouds. Additionally, we observe that TPC also boosts performance on standard datasets like ModelNet40 and ShapeNetPart. The source code for this project is available at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/TPC.

Our findings indicate that the VSI is suppressed when dust growth occurs in the disk's midplane, a scenario that aligns with observations of low turbulence in the outer zones of T Tauri stars. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the VSI can be reactivated in the disk's upper layers if dust growth is accompanied by a significant increase in the dust-to-gas mass ratio. These results suggest that dust evolution plays a crucial role in regulating the VSI and that the instability's impact on angular momentum transport is contingent upon the local dust-to-gas mass ratio. Consequently, the VSI may be more effective at driving gas accretion in the outer regions of disks where the dust-to-gas mass ratio is elevated. The convergence of artificial intelligence and blockchain technologies has significantly advanced the development of intelligent transportation systems. In Internet of Vehicles (IoV) environments, the rapid growth of data volume and the increasing complexity of data processing have created significant challenges for traditional data management and privacy protection methods. Consequently, there is an urgent need to explore new solutions for data management and privacy preservation in IoV systems. Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising approach to address these issues, offering a viable solution for privacy concerns in IoVs. However, the decentralized nature of FL introduces new vulnerabilities, such as data poisoning attacks, which can compromise the integrity of the learning process. To counteract these risks, blockchain technology can be integrated with FL to create a more secure framework. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of recent advancements in blockchain-enabled federated learning frameworks designed for IoVs. We examine the underlying principles of both technologies, analyze the specific challenges associated with integrating them in IoV contexts, and review various proposed solutions. Furthermore, we discuss the limitations of current approaches and outline potential future research directions. This survey aims to offer a clear understanding of how blockchain and federated learning can be effectively combined to enhance the security and privacy of IoV systems. The primary contributions of this work are detailed as follows. First, we introduce the fundamental concepts of blockchain and federated learning, along with their respective advantages and limitations. Second, we identify the key challenges involved in implementing blockchain-empowered federated learning within IoVs. Third, we present a taxonomy of existing solutions that integrate blockchain with federated learning for IoVs, analyzing their strengths and weaknesses. Finally, we highlight the limitations of current methods and propose future research directions. By clarifying the integration of blockchain and federated learning in IoVs, this survey provides valuable insights for developing more secure and privacy-preserving intelligent transportation systems. The taxonomy of blockchain-empowered federated learning frameworks for IoVs is illustrated in Figure 1. The remaining sections of this paper are organized as follows: Section 2 offers an overview of blockchain technology; Section 3 covers federated learning; Section 4 discusses the challenges of integrating blockchain with federated learning in IoVs; Section 5 reviews existing solutions; Section 6 outlines future research directions; and Section 7 concludes the paper.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a deep learning architecture widely adopted for video identification tasks due to their capacity to model temporal dependencies. These findings are derived through a combination of a virial identity and a local existence result. The analysis relies on a reflection method to extend the solution into the interior of the obstacle, where the solution is defined as zero. This approach is applicable to a particular type of nonlinearity, which we refer to as a "reflected" nonlinearity. Lobster-eye optics, characterized by a reflective, quasi-one-dimensional focusing structure, are well-suited for wide-field X-ray monitoring. This study introduces a novel multiplexing approach to enhance the field of view of lobster-eye instruments. We present a design for a multi-tiered system that combines multiple lobster-eye modules with a central, large-area detector. This configuration enables the creation of a wide-field imaging spectrometer with a field of view exceeding 100 degrees. The design leverages the inherent angular resolution of the lobster-eye modules to achieve a high-resolution focal line on the central detector, which is then dispersed by a diffraction grating. This allows for the reconstruction of the full two-dimensional spectrum for each point within the field of view. We detail the design and simulation of a multi-tiered system with a 100-degree field of view, utilizing three 20-degree modules and a central detector with a 1.5-meter focal length. The resulting system achieves an angular resolution of 1.5 degrees and an energy resolution of 10% at 6 keV. We also describe the construction of a smaller-scale prototype featuring a 30-degree field of view, which will be tested at the 2024 Laboratory for X-Ray Astrophysics (LXRA) workshop. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this multi-tiered architecture for wide-field X-ray monitoring. The proposed system could serve as a powerful instrument for detecting transient events, such as flares from magnetars and black holes, and for monitoring variable sources like Tidal Disruption Events (TDEs) and Fast X-ray Transients (FXRs). Furthermore, it could act as a rapid-response telescope for follow-up observations of TDEs and FXRs detected by wide-field monitors like the Einstein@Home (E@H) project. This multi-tiered design could also be adapted for other focusing optics, such as Wolter-I telescopes, to create wide-field imaging spectrometers. Such systems would be valuable for monitoring transient events and for performing spectroscopic observations of sources that are too faint for traditional imaging spectrometers. Ultimately, this multi-tiered architecture could be scaled up to develop a wide-field imaging spectrometer with a field of view surpassing 200 degrees. Such an instrument would be an ideal addition to future X-ray observatories, including the proposed IXPE-N extension, Athena, and the Cosmic X-ray Observatory (CXO).

We present a relativistic first principles approach to investigate the electronic structure of magnetic impurities and their associated Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states on superconducting surfaces. Utilizing the linearized augmented plane wave (LAPW) method, we explicitly incorporate the superconducting order parameter into the Hamiltonian via a Bogoliubov--de Gennes (BdG) formalism. This enables a detailed analysis of the YSR states for a single Mn adatom and various Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface. Our results indicate that the spin polarization of the YSR states is sensitive to the specific Mn cluster configuration. Furthermore, we observe that the energy splitting between the two YSR states increases as the distance between Mn atoms in the cluster grows. These findings offer valuable insights into the electronic structure of magnetic impurities and their YSR states on superconducting surfaces. The proposed first principles methodology is broadly applicable to studying YSR states in diverse impurity configurations on superconducting surfaces. We introduce the minimal extension of the simplest scoto-seesaw framework capable of generating a high neutrino scale via the seesaw mechanism and achieving a dark matter (DM) mass of 100 GeV through the freeze-out mechanism. This model features the minimal set of additional particles required to satisfy these conditions. We demonstrate that the dark sector, comprising the singlet scalar and the new right-handed neutrinos, exhibits a first-order phase transition. Furthermore, we identify the parameter space where the electroweak vacuum remains stable up to the Planck scale. Our analysis reveals that the thermal production of DM is closely linked to vacuum stability, with the DM mass serving as the primary determinant of this connection. Additionally, we find that vacuum stability imposes a lower bound on the singlet scalar mass, which in turn sets an upper limit on the neutrino scale. Finally, we present a comprehensive phenomenological study of the simplest scoto-seesaw model, focusing on the most accessible dark sector processes at the LHC. These processes include singlet scalar decays into invisible neutrinos and into pairs of new right-handed neutrinos, as well as the production of new right-handed neutrinos via singlet scalar decays and direct pair production. We also examine the potential for dark sector cascade decays to generate detectable displaced vertices at the LHC. Our findings indicate that the thermal production of DM and the generation of displaced vertices are mutually exclusive in this model. Consequently, the simplest scoto-seesaw model can only satisfy all cosmological and experimental constraints if the DM mass is approximately 10 GeV, a scenario that would likely evade detection at the LHC. This result suggests that more complex extensions of the scoto-seesaw framework are necessary to simultaneously achieve a 100 GeV dark matter mass, a stable vacuum, and observable dark sector phenomena at the LHC.
